title: Salok Sehskriti
hook: verses in a Sanskrit-flavored style, on the passing world (ang 1353)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Bavan Akhri closed, a long alphabet that ends in grace. When you finished something, did you notice what was given along the way? Day one thousand two hundred three.

Some words wear a robe. Say "thou" instead of "you", or "hath" instead of "has", and the room changes: the sentence sounds older, more formal, like it came from a temple instead of a kitchen. Near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, from Ang thirteen hundred fifty-three, there's a set of verses that does exactly that. They're called Salok Sehskriti, and their words wear the robe of an old learned language. They sound different from the pages around them. Today, just listening for how it sounds.
screen: `SOME WORDS WEAR A ROBE.` → `ANG 1353.` → `A DIFFERENT SOUND.`

segments.voice: Sehskriti, sometimes spelled Sahaskriti, names the style. The outline calls it Sanskrit-flavored, and that's the plain way to say it: these are not verses in classical Sanskrit, but in a speech dressed in its endings and its weight. Lines close on sounds like ang and ah, so the ear hears something stately and old. Guru Nanak's saloks open the set, and Guru Arjan's verses follow. So here's the surprise. Sanskrit was the language of learned pandits and temple scholarship. On the pages around these verses, the Gurus sing in the speech of ordinary people. Yet here the Gurus pick up that learned register and use it. Why? The text doesn't explain itself. Some readers suggest it speaks to the learned in their own manner. Others hear it simply as range: the Guru can sing in the village voice and the scholar's voice, and say the same truth in both. What the verses say, in that robe, is not new. Paraphrased, they keep turning to how quickly this world passes and how only remembering the Lord stays. The dress is grand. The message is the one Sikhs hear everywhere in the Granth. That's the lesson of the style itself. A learned language doesn't make the Name truer, and a plain one doesn't make it smaller. The Guru wears whichever robe reaches the listener, and the body underneath is the same.
screen: `A SANSKRIT-FLAVORED STYLE.` · `GURU NANAK, THEN GURU ARJAN.` · `THE LEARNED VOICE, PICKED UP.` · `GRAND DRESS, SAME MESSAGE.` · then, large: `THE OLD TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read two verses. If you can find the Salok Sehskriti, starting on Ang thirteen hundred fifty-three, read two of them aloud, slowly, in Gurmukhi if you can, or in transliteration. Don't worry about understanding every word. Listen to the endings, the weight of the sound, the way it differs from everyday speech. Then sit with the breath and let the sound fade. If you can't find them, sit and listen to the plainest sound near you, a fan, a bird, traffic, and notice that it, too, is a voice. The bell holds the time.
Salok Sehskriti. Verses near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib in a Sanskrit-flavored style, speaking of the passing world. Today's word.
Your line: the old tongue. Today, notice when someone dresses up their words, or dresses them down, and listen past the robe for what they actually mean. Day one thousand two hundred three.

howItsDone: The Salok Sehskriti of Guru Nanak and Guru Arjan are part of the closing sections of the Guru Granth Sahib; they are read in full during an akhand path or sahaj path, and some Sikhs study them with a giani's help because of their unusual vocabulary.

fork.setup: you're a Guru with a truth to sing, and the learned of your day speak a grand, old language. what do the Salok Sehskriti do?
options: refuse that language and use only plain speech.
pick up the learned style and say the same truth in it.
invent a new teaching to suit the grand style.
fork.reveal: the Gurus wear the learned robe here, and the message underneath is the same one sung in the people's speech.

original.note: the heading of these verses on Ang 1353: the old, learned-sounding style.

trapdoor: what you thought: sehskriti is just another name for Sanskrit.
what it means: it names a style, everyday speech dressed in Sanskrit's endings and weight.
what a scholar hears: the Gurus can sing in the people's tongue and the learned register, with one message in both.
recall: the letter S, the Patti's first
